chunks: "After the board comes out of the reflow oven, I'd expect roughly this sequence.
First, visual and automated optical inspection to catch anything obviously wrong, like missing or skewed parts or bridges, and X-ray on boards with BGAs.

Then an unpowered electrical test, either in-circuit test or flying probe, which checks for shorts, opens, and the values of resistors, capacitors and diodes, without turning the board on, so a short on a power rail can't damage anything.
Next, the first power-up, with a current-limited supply, so if something is wrong the supply folds back instead of burning parts.
Then programming: flash the firmware, load calibration constants and write the serial number.

After that, the functional test: check that the voltage rails come up in the right order and levels, the oscillator runs, the processor boots, communication buses work, sensors and outputs behave, and measure things like current draw.
For mains-powered products there's a safety test like hipot, and some products get burn-in.
Finally, labeling, final visual inspection and packing, with all results logged under the serial number. The logic is cheap and safe first, expensive and powered last.
Failing boards go to a repair station, then get retested from the start."
